learning_goal: Divide the primitive gut into foregut, midgut and hindgut at their exact boundaries, name the artery and the vertebral level of each, list what each division becomes, and use those three divisions to place referred pain and to explain oesophageal atresia, duodenal atresia, malrotation, Hirschsprung disease and imperforate anus.

terms: junction of proximal two thirds and distal one third of transverse colon

structures.name: Buccopharyngeal membrane
structures.label: Buccopharyngeal membrane
structures.narration: At each end of the tube, ectoderm and endoderm touch with no mesoderm between them, and those two-layered spots are the buccopharyngeal membrane at the head and the cloacal membrane at the tail. The buccopharyngeal ruptures in week four to open the mouth, the cloacal in week seven to open the anus and urogenital tract. A membrane that never ruptures is an atresia — choanal or oesophageal at one end, imperforate anus at the other.

structures.name: Caecal bud
structures.label: Caecal bud
structures.narration: Midgut: duodenum beyond the papilla, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. Superior mesenteric artery, lesser splanchnic nerve at T10 and T11, and therefore periumbilical pain — which is exactly why early appendicitis hurts around the umbilicus before it moves to the right iliac fossa.
terms: proximal two thirds of transverse colon

structures.name: Cloaca
structures.label: Cloaca
structures.narration: The hindgut ends in a common chamber, the cloaca. A wedge of mesoderm, the urorectal septum, grows down and splits it into an anorectal canal behind and a urogenital sinus in front, meeting the cloacal membrane at what becomes the perineal body. The ectodermal proctodeum then meets the endoderm from inside, and their meeting point is the pectinate line.

structures.name: Duodenum — spans the foregut/midgut boundary
structures.label: Duodenum — spans the foregut/midgut boundary
structures.narration: In week six the proliferating epithelium temporarily plugs the lumen in places, especially the duodenum, and it must recanalize by about week eight. Fail completely and you get an atresia; fail partly and you get a stenosis. Remember the mechanism by region: duodenal atresia is a failure of recanalization, while jejunal and ileal atresia are usually a vascular accident in a segment that had already opened.

structures.name: Foregut
structures.label: Foregut
structures.narration: Foregut: oesophagus, stomach, duodenum as far as the papilla, and the organs that bud off it — liver and biliary tree from the hepatic diverticulum, both pancreatic buds, and the respiratory diverticulum that becomes trachea and lungs. All supplied by the coeliac trunk, all sensed through the greater splanchnic nerve from T5 to T9, which is why foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium.

structures.name: Hindgut
structures.label: Hindgut
structures.narration: Hindgut: distal third of the transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum and the anal canal down to the pectinate line. Inferior mesenteric artery, least splanchnic nerve at T12, hypogastric or suprapubic pain. The pectinate line is a germ-layer boundary, and it is why everything above it differs from everything below it in blood supply, venous drainage, lymphatics and sensation.
terms: distal one third of transverse colon
upper part of the urogenital sinus

structures.name: Midgut
structures.label: Midgut
structures.narration: The gut is divided into foregut, midgut and hindgut, and the division is arterial, not anatomical convenience. Coeliac trunk at T12 for the foregut, superior mesenteric at L1 for the midgut, inferior mesenteric at L3 for the hindgut. Learn the three arteries and their levels first; every boundary, every pattern of referred pain and half the surgical anatomy of the abdomen falls out of them.

structures.name: Major duodenal papilla (foregut/midgut boundary)
structures.label: Major duodenal papilla (foregut/midgut boundary)
structures.narration: The foregut ends and the midgut begins in the second part of the duodenum, exactly where the bile duct opens at the major duodenal papilla. That is why the duodenum has a double blood supply from both the coeliac and superior mesenteric territories: the boundary runs through the middle of it.

structures.name: Vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
structures.label: Vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
structures.narration: Where the midgut still opens into the yolk sac, folding narrows the connection to a thin vitelline duct at the apex of the midgut loop. It should regress completely. When it does not, the commonest remnant is a Meckel diverticulum — a true diverticulum of the ileum, often with ectopic gastric mucosa, classically presenting as painless rectal bleeding in a small child.

structures.name: Transverse colon 2/3 point (midgut/hindgut boundary)
structures.label: Transverse colon 2/3 point (midgut/hindgut boundary)
structures.narration: The midgut ends at the junction of the proximal two thirds and the distal one third of the transverse colon. That is the arterial watershed between superior and inferior mesenteric territories, and it is why ischaemic colitis has a favourite site near the left colic flexure.
terms: junction of proximal two thirds and distal one third

structures.name: Malrotation — the turn stopped at 90 degrees
structures.label: Malrotation — the turn stopped at 90 degrees
structures.narration: If the two hundred and seventy degree rotation is incomplete, the caecum never reaches the right iliac fossa and the mesentery stays attached over a narrow base instead of a broad oblique line. A narrow base is a pivot: the whole midgut can twist on the superior mesenteric artery and infarct within hours. Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until imaging proves otherwise, and it is a surgical emergency, not an outpatient problem.
terms: caecum in the right upper quadrant

structures.name: High anorectal malformation — the septum stopped short
structures.label: High anorectal malformation — the septum stopped short
structures.narration: At the tail end, two things can go wrong. The anal membrane may simply fail to rupture, giving a low lesion with a normally placed but covered anus. Or the urorectal septum may fail to reach the cloacal membrane, leaving the rectum communicating with the urinary tract or vagina — a high lesion with a fistula. Meconium appearing in the urine or at the vulva is what tells you which. As with oesophageal atresia, examine for the rest of the VACTERL association.

structures.name: Aganglionic segment — the crest front stopped at s = 0.86
structures.label: Aganglionic segment — the crest front stopped at s = 0.86
structures.narration: Neural crest cells colonise the gut from the top down, so when migration fails it is the last segment that is left bare. That makes Hirschsprung disease always involve the rectum and extend proximally, most often only as far as the rectosigmoid. The aganglionic segment cannot relax, so it stays narrow and the normal bowel above it dilates — the megacolon is the healthy part. Failure to pass meconium in the first forty-eight hours is the clue, and the diagnosis is made on rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells.

views.title: One tube from mouth to anus
views.narration: Start with the whole tube in side view, sealed at the head by the buccopharyngeal membrane and at the tail by the cloacal membrane, with the yolk sac still hanging from its middle. It is endoderm rolled up by the folds of week four. Endoderm gives the lining and the glands, splanchnic mesoderm gives the muscle and the peritoneum, and neural crest cells arrive later to supply the nerve cells. Three sources, three sets of diseases.

views.title: Three arteries cut the tube into three
views.narration: Now put the arteries on. Coeliac trunk at T12, superior mesenteric at L1, inferior mesenteric at L3. The boundaries are exactly where one territory hands over to the next: the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, and the junction of the proximal two thirds and distal one third of the transverse colon. Those are the two sentences to memorise verbatim — every derivative list and every referred pain answer depends on them.

views.title: Close up: the three arterial origins
views.narration: The same three arteries, with the aorta taken away so that the only thing left to look at is the spacing. Coeliac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, in that order from the head down, each one reaching forward from the midline into its own division of the tube. Nothing else in this scene is arranged in a line like this, and the order is the whole of the fact: whatever an artery supplies, it supplies because the tube was cut there first.

views.title: Close up: the two boundaries
views.narration: Now the two beads on their own. The upper one is the major duodenal papilla, in the second part of the duodenum, where the foregut hands over to the midgut. The lower one is the point two thirds of the way along the transverse colon, where the midgut hands over to the hindgut. Everything a question can ask about this topic — which artery, which derivative, where the pain is felt, which malformation — is decided by which side of one of these two beads a structure sits on. views.title: What each division becomes
views.narration: Run down the tube once, division by division. Foregut to the papilla, with the liver, gallbladder, pancreas and the lung bud all budding off it. Midgut to two thirds along the transverse colon, carrying the appendix and the vitelline duct. Hindgut to the pectinate line, ending in the cloaca. Then attach the nerve to each: greater splanchnic T5 to T9 for the foregut and epigastric pain, lesser splanchnic T10 to T11 for the midgut and periumbilical pain, least splanchnic T12 for the hindgut and suprapubic pain. That is why appendicitis starts at the umbilicus.

claims.claim: the turn is under way at this stage

views.title: Close up: the liver and pancreas bud off the duodenum
views.narration: The foregut is the division that grows organs off its own wall, and this is the frame that shows them: the camera is on the duodenum, because all three of these buds leave the tube within a few millimetres of the papilla. The hepatic diverticulum reaches forward and becomes liver and biliary tree. Behind it the dorsal pancreatic bud, and ventrally the smaller bud that swings round to join it — one gland from two buds, which is why an annular pancreas can ring the duodenum. All of them hang off the tube ABOVE the papilla, which is why all of them are foregut, coeliac territory, and epigastric pain. This is also the stage at which the duodenal lumen between them is a solid cord of epithelium, which is the next beat but one.

views.narration: Highest of the foregut buds, and the only one that stops being gut. The respiratory diverticulum grows off the ventral wall of the foregut and is then separated from it by the tracheo-oesophageal septum, leaving trachea in front and oesophagus behind. When that septum fails the two stay joined: oesophageal atresia with a tracheo-oesophageal fistula, polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot swallow, and a tube that will not pass. It is the first disease in this scene's list of failures, and this is the structure it happens to.

views.narration: The duodenum with its wall dropped back to almost nothing, so that what is inside it can be seen. Between about week five and week eight the lining proliferates until it fills the channel completely and the duodenum is a solid cord of epithelium: the pale core is that cord, and there is no lumen drawn beside it because at this instant there is none to draw. It must recanalize by week eight. When it does not, the duodenum stays obstructed exactly here — duodenal atresia, the double bubble on the film, and the association with Down syndrome. The plug is local to the duodenum, which is the whole of why duodenal atresia is a recanalization failure and jejunal or ileal atresia is not.

views.title: The midgut leaves the abdomen and comes back turned
views.narration: Only the midgut rotates, and only because it runs out of room. It herniates into the cord at about week six, turning ninety degrees anticlockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, and returns by about week ten with a further one hundred and eighty degrees — two hundred and seventy in total, all anticlockwise, viewed from the front. The caecum lands in the right iliac fossa and the mesentery is left attached along a broad oblique line. Both of those facts matter when the failures are listed.

views.title: Opening the two ends
views.narration: Cut the embryo in the midline and look at the two ends. The buccopharyngeal membrane ruptures in week four, the cloacal in week seven, and before that rupture the urorectal septum has already split the cloaca into anorectal canal and urogenital sinus. In the middle of the tube, the duodenal lumen is temporarily plugged by proliferating epithelium and must reopen by week eight. Three events, three sets of atresias — and knowing which mechanism belongs to which region is what the question is actually testing.

views.narration: The caudal end with the chamber wall taken off, because the septum and the two channels it makes are INSIDE the cloaca and no camera can see them through it. views.title: Where each division fails
views.narration: Walk down the tube one more time and hang a disease on each step. Foregut septation fails: oesophageal atresia with a fistula, polyhydramnios, a tube that will not pass. Recanalization fails: duodenal atresia, double bubble, think of Down syndrome. Rotation fails: malrotation, and a narrow mesenteric base that lets the midgut twist — bilious vomiting in a neonate is an emergency. Neural crest migration fails: Hirschsprung, always involving the rectum, diagnosed by biopsy. The cloacal end fails: imperforate anus, with a fistula if the lesion is high. One tube, one developmental step each, and the whole paediatric surgical list in order.

deferred_beats.title: One tube, made by folding
deferred_beats.narration: The primitive gut is not a new organ. It is the roof of the yolk sac, rolled into a tube by the head, tail and lateral folds during week four. Hold that in mind and the whole gut becomes one tube that was cut into three by its blood supply.
deferred_beats.why_not_a_view: The folding that makes the tube is the subject of lateral-folding and cranio-caudal-folding, which model it. This model begins with the tube already closed, so a beat here would draw the same frame as beat 1 and teach it worse than the scenes that own it.

deferred_beats.title: Endoderm lines it, splanchnic mesoderm builds it
deferred_beats.narration: Two germ layers build the gut and it is worth being exact about which does what. Endoderm gives only the epithelial lining and the glands that bud from it. Splanchnic mesoderm gives the muscle, the connective tissue and the visceral peritoneum. The nerve cells come from neither — neural crest cells migrate in to form the enteric plexuses, and when they fail to arrive you get Hirschsprung disease.
deferred_beats.why_not_a_view: This model carries no wall layers — it is a lumen and a calibre, not an endoderm and a splanchnic mesoderm. Drawing a beat for layers it does not build would be a caption over an unchanged picture.

deferred_beats.title: The midgut loop, its hernia and its turn
deferred_beats.narration: Only the midgut does something dramatic. Around week six the loop outgrows the abdomen and herniates into the umbilical cord, rotating ninety degrees anticlockwise around the superior mesenteric artery on the way out. It returns by about week ten, rotating a further one hundred and eighty degrees, so the total is two hundred and seventy degrees anticlockwise. That rotation is what carries the caecum to the right iliac fossa and lays the duodenum and the ascending and descending colon against the back wall.
terms: superior mesenteric artery is the axis
deferred_beats.why_not_a_view: Split across beats 4 and 5, which draw the hernia at its measured peak and the fixed arrangement at t = 1. The words are carried on those two views rather than here.

deferred_beats.title: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
deferred_beats.narration: The respiratory diverticulum buds off the foregut and is separated from it by the tracheo-oesophageal septum. When that septum forms incompletely the oesophagus ends blind and usually communicates with the trachea below — the common variant is a proximal blind pouch with a distal fistula. Suspect it before birth from polyhydramnios, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid, and after birth when a nasogastric tube will not pass and the first feed causes choking. Look for the rest of the VACTERL group.
deferred_beats.why_not_a_view: The respiratory diverticulum is built, but the tracheo-oesophageal septum that fails in this lesion is tracheoesophageal-septum’s own queue item and is not modelled here. A beat would be a caption over the normal foregut.

deferred_beats.title: Duodenal atresia — the double bubble
deferred_beats.narration: Duodenal atresia is the recanalization failure, and it is the one tied to Down syndrome. The plain film shows a double bubble — stomach and proximal duodenum both distended, nothing beyond. The vomiting is bilious because the obstruction is usually distal to the major duodenal papilla. Annular pancreas, where the ventral bud encircles the duodenum, produces the same picture from outside.

WHAT THE BEAT DOES: the cord is inside the duodenum, and the only way viz3d shows the inside of a TAUGHT structure is ISOLATE_REGION's ghost — viz3d.js:2409 sets `ghosting` from state.ghosted and :2418 then drops every structure that is not highlighted or selected to min(0.10, authored opacity). So the duodenum is drawn at 0.10 and the plug, which is the one highlighted thing, at 1.0. WHY measure-scene-visibility CANNOT SEE THAT: it reimplements viz3d's ops rather than driving it, and its painting applies ONLY each structure's AUTHORED opacity — measure-scene-visibility.mjs:308, `if (o.material && s.opacity != null) { o.material.opacity = s.opacity; }`. The duodenum authors no opacity, so the tool draws the wall fully opaque and both its id-pick and its alpha-aware pass read the cord as zero (peak 0). The tool's own header says this reimplementation is its one weakness and that where the two disagree, viz3d is right. THE MEASUREMENT THAT COUNTS: walk-scene-in-player.mjs loads viz3d.js, mounts the scene and clicks the view chip, so the ghost is the player's own code; it reads duod_plug at 2.783% of the frame and 41.6% of this beat's subject, with the duodenum at 4.847% and the papilla at 1.578%, frame still, 0 px drift.
